posts.title: Agent demos vs agent systems
posts.hook: Every agent demo I've seen this month breaks the same way in production.
posts.body:
Every agent demo I've seen this month breaks the same way in production.

The LLM call works. The tool calls work. The happy path is beautiful.

Then you hit the first ambiguous edge case and the whole thing falls over because there's no deterministic fallback. No retry logic that actually understands what failed. No structured output validation before the next step fires.

I run Claude Code agents across my entire GTM pipeline. Enrichment, email infrastructure, CRM writes, content dispatch. The part that makes it work isn't the model. It's the 200 lines of boring Python around it.

Schema validation on every tool call return. Idempotent writes so a retry doesn't double-create records. A secrets table in SQLite instead of .env files that drift across machines. Structured error handling that tells the agent what went wrong in a format it can actually reason about.

The unglamorous stuff is the whole game. The model is maybe 20% of why my agents work reliably. The other 80% is the harness.

If your agent works in a demo but not in a cron job running at midnight with no human watching... you don't have an agent. You have a notebook cell.

remixes.label: the-boring-middle
remixes.hook: The space between a working LLM call and a production agent system is 90% unglamorous plumbing.
remixes.body:
The space between a working LLM call and a production agent system is 90% unglamorous plumbing.

I call it the boring middle. It's the retry logic that knows the difference between a rate limit and a malformed request. It's the output validator that catches when the model returns a confident answer in the wrong schema. It's the fallback path that routes to a deterministic function when the LLM hallucinates a tool call that doesn't exist.

None of this shows up in demos. Demos show the happy path because the happy path is genuinely impressive. The model reasons, calls tools, chains steps together. Beautiful.

But production traffic includes the customer who submits an emoji-only input. The API that returns a 500 on the third call in a sequence. The model that confidently picks a tool parameter that violates a business rule.

I've shipped agent systems that run thousands of tasks weekly. The LLM logic is maybe 20% of the codebase. The rest is error boundaries, state machines, structured output parsing, and dead-letter queues for failed runs.

The teams building reliable agents aren't better at prompting. They're better at plumbing.
remixes.cta: What's the least glamorous piece of your agent stack that you couldn't live without?

remixes.label: demo-day-hangover
remixes.hook: I watched a founder demo a flawless AI agent on Tuesday. By Friday their engineering lead sent me a Slack message: "It's broken in seven ways we didn't anticipate."
remixes.body:
I watched a founder demo a flawless AI agent on Tuesday. By Friday their engineering lead sent me a Slack message: "It's broken in seven ways we didn't anticipate."

Here's what broke. Real users sent ambiguous inputs the demo never covered. An upstream API changed its response format. The agent called the right tool with the wrong parameters and nobody validated the output before the next step consumed it. Three runs hit a race condition and wrote conflicting data.

Every single failure was in the connective tissue, not the AI.

This pattern repeats everywhere. The model is not the bottleneck. The system around the model is. Error handling, state management, input validation, output parsing, idempotency, observability.

I run agents in production daily. My rule: if you can't explain what happens when step 3 of 5 fails, you don't have an agent system. You have a demo.

The fix isn't more sophisticated prompting. It's treating agent orchestration like real software engineering. Typed interfaces between steps. Deterministic fallbacks. Structured logging that tells you exactly where and why a run failed.

Production agents are built on boring engineering, not clever prompts.

posts.title: Evals beat model selection
posts.hook: I spent two weeks picking the perfect model for my enrichment pipeline. Should've spent two hours on evals instead.
posts.body:
I spent two weeks picking the perfect model for my enrichment pipeline. Should've spent two hours on evals instead.

The pipeline takes a company domain, pulls public signals, and classifies fit against an ICP. I tested Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, GPT-4o. Obsessed over which one "got it" better.

Then I built a 50-row eval set with known answers. Ran all four models against it.

Sonnet and Opus scored within 3% of each other. The actual variance came from prompt structure and the data I was feeding in. Garbage enrichment data in, garbage classification out, regardless of model.

So I stopped model shopping and started fixing my inputs. Cleaned up the scraping. Added a validation step before classification. Wrote five prompt variants and scored them against the eval set.

Accuracy went from 71% to 89%. On the same model I started with.

The companies actually shipping with AI aren't chasing the frontier model announcement every week. They're writing eval sets, measuring what breaks, and fixing the system around the model.

Models are commoditizing fast. Your eval harness and data quality are the moat.

remixes.label: vibes-vs-data
remixes.hook: "This model just feels smarter" is the most expensive sentence in AI right now.
remixes.body:
"This model just feels smarter" is the most expensive sentence in AI right now.

I watched myself do this with an enrichment pipeline. Tested four models. Read the outputs. Picked the one whose answers "felt" most complete. Almost shipped it.

Then I forced myself to build something simple: 50 rows of company domains with known ICP classifications. Ground truth. Not opinions.

Ran all four models against the same set. Measured precision and recall on the classification task.

The model that "felt" best? It was verbose and confident, which made its answers read well. But it misclassified 11 out of 50 companies. The model I almost dismissed scored within 2 points of the top performer and cost a fraction per call.

Vibes testing rewards confidence and fluency. Eval sets reward correctness. These are completely different things.

The 50-row eval set took me about two hours to build. Pulling real examples from our CRM where the classification was already known. That two-hour investment has saved me from three bad model decisions since.

You don't need a fancy eval framework. You need a spreadsheet with inputs and correct answers. Run your models. Count the right answers. That's it.
remixes.cta: What's stopping you from building a basic eval set this week?

remixes.label: eval-set-recipe
remixes.hook: Here's the exact process I use to build an eval set in under two hours. It's changed how I make every AI decision.
remixes.body:
Here's the exact process I use to build an eval set in under two hours. It's changed how I make every AI decision.

Step one: pick 50 real inputs from your production data. Not synthetic. Not edge cases you invented. Actual inputs your system processes.

Step two: label them with correct outputs. For my enrichment pipeline, this meant pulling companies where I already knew the ICP classification from closed deals in the CRM. For a summarization task, it might mean writing the correct summary yourself.

Step three: run every model candidate against the same 50 inputs with the same prompt. Log every output.

Step four: score mechanically. Did the output match? Partially match? Miss completely? No subjective judgment. Binary or categorical scoring only.

I did this for a company classification pipeline. Tested Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, GPT-4o. My gut said Opus was clearly best. The eval showed Sonnet scored within 2 points and cost significantly less per call. That insight paid for itself in the first month of production usage.

The eval set also becomes your regression test. Every time you change the prompt, rerun the set. If accuracy drops, you know immediately.

Two hours of labeling. Months of confident decisions.

posts.title: Claude Code replaced my orchestration scripts
posts.hook: I deleted 600 lines of orchestration Python last month. Replaced it with a CLAUDE.md file and a cron job.
posts.body:
I deleted 600 lines of orchestration Python last month. Replaced it with a CLAUDE.md file and a cron job.

The old setup: a Python script that pulled enrichment data from four APIs, cleaned it, scored it, wrote to SQLite, then triggered email sequences. Every API change broke something. Every new data source meant refactoring the pipeline.

Now: Claude Code reads the CLAUDE.md (which describes the schema, the scoring logic, the API contracts), runs the pipeline, and handles the edge cases inline. When an API returns unexpected data, it reasons about it instead of throwing a KeyError at 2am.

The shift that made this work wasn't "use AI." It was treating the agent like a junior dev who needs extremely clear written instructions. The CLAUDE.md is basically an onboarding doc. Here's the database schema. Here's what good data looks like. Here's what to do when enrichment returns null. Here are the accounts and credentials to use.

The more precise the instructions, the more autonomous the agent. That's the actual unlock. Not the model capability. The context engineering.

My daily cron has run 47 straight days without a manual intervention.

remixes.body:
My most important production file isn't code. It's a markdown document that tells an AI agent what to do.

I used to maintain a 600-line Python orchestration script. It pulled data from four APIs, cleaned it, scored it, wrote to SQLite, then triggered email sequences. Standard pipeline stuff.

Every API change broke something. Every new data source meant refactoring. I spent more time maintaining the glue code than improving the actual logic.

Now I have a CLAUDE.md file that describes the pipeline in plain English. What data to pull. How to validate it. What the scoring criteria are. Where to write the output. Claude Code reads it and executes accordingly.

The shift: instead of encoding logic in brittle Python, I describe intent in a structured document. The agent handles the implementation details. When an API changes its response format, I update one line in the doc instead of refactoring three functions.

This isn't about being lazy. The CLAUDE.md file has strict rules. Schema definitions. Validation requirements. Fallback instructions. It's a contract, not a wish list.

But it's a contract written in English instead of Python. And that means non-technical teammates can read it, review it, and suggest changes.

The instruction document is becoming the new codebase.

remixes.hook: My orchestration pipeline used to break every two weeks. I deleted it. It hasn't broken since.
remixes.body:
My orchestration pipeline used to break every two weeks. I deleted it. It hasn't broken since.

The old system: 600 lines of Python gluing together four APIs, a scoring function, SQLite writes, and email triggers. Worked fine until it didn't. An API would change a field name. A response format would shift. A new data source would require a schema migration and three function refactors.

Maintenance cost was eating the productivity the pipeline was supposed to create.

So I tried something different. Wrote a detailed instruction file describing what the pipeline should do. Inputs, outputs, validation rules, scoring logic, error handling. Hooked it up to Claude Code on a cron job.

First week: nervous. Checked outputs obsessively. Everything matched or exceeded the old pipeline's accuracy.

First month: an API changed its response format. The agent adapted because the instruction file describes what the data means, not how to parse a specific JSON structure. Zero maintenance on my end.

Three months in: I've added two new data sources by adding paragraphs to the instruction file. No code changes. No refactoring.

The maintenance cost flipped from growing linearly with complexity to staying nearly flat. That's the real win.

posts.title: Agent permissions are the real bottleneck
posts.hook: My agent can write to Attio, send emails via Gmail, push to GitHub, and query four databases. The scariest part isn't what it can do. It's what it can do wrong.
posts.body:
My agent can write to Attio, send emails via Gmail, push to GitHub, and query four databases. The scariest part isn't what it can do. It's what it can do wrong.

I have multiple Google accounts, multiple Notion workspaces, multiple API tenants. Early on, my agent exported data from the wrong account. Searched the wrong mailbox. Almost deployed to the wrong Vercel project.

So I built an identity routing table. Before any read or write, the agent resolves which identity to use, echoes it back, and waits. Outbound sends are gated behind an explicit approval flag.

This is the unsexy infrastructure layer that nobody's building yet. We're all excited about giving agents more capabilities. But capability without scoped permissions is a liability.

Your agent doesn't need access to everything. It needs the minimum access for the current task, with clear boundaries on what it can touch. Same principle as IAM roles, applied to AI.

The teams that figure out agent identity and permission scoping first are going to move 10x faster than the ones still debugging "why did the agent email the wrong list from the wrong account."

remixes.label: identity-crisis
remixes.hook: My AI agent emailed the wrong client from the wrong account. That's when I realized permissions aren't a feature. They're the foundation.
remixes.body:
My AI agent emailed the wrong client from the wrong account. That's when I realized permissions aren't a feature. They're the foundation.

I run multiple businesses. Multiple Google accounts, multiple CRM workspaces, multiple API tenants. My agent has access to all of them because it needs to work across contexts.

Early on, the failures were quiet. The agent exported data from Account A when it should have used Account B. Searched the wrong Gmail inbox. Almost pushed code to the wrong repository. Each mistake was plausible enough that the agent didn't flag it.

So I built what I call an identity routing table. A simple markdown file that maps every service to the correct account, credential, and access scope. Before any read or write operation, the agent resolves the identity from this file and echoes it back: "TARGET: Gmail as clearbox via oauth-token-3."

If two credentials could match and the routing table doesn't disambiguate, the agent stops and asks. No guessing.

This sounds trivially simple. It is. That's the point. The solution to agent permission chaos isn't a sophisticated RBAC system. It's a lookup table and a hard rule: resolve before acting, never assume.

The scariest agent bugs aren't the ones that fail loudly. They're the ones that succeed confidently in the wrong context.
remixes.cta: Have your agents ever taken a correct action against the wrong target?

remixes.label: blast-radius-thinking
remixes.hook: Every tool you give an AI agent is a loaded gun pointed at your production systems. The question isn't whether it can shoot. It's whether it knows which direction to aim.
remixes.body:
Every tool you give an AI agent is a loaded gun pointed at your production systems. The question isn't whether it can shoot. It's whether it knows which direction to aim.

I give my agent write access to a CRM, email sending, GitHub push, and four databases. It needs all of these to do its job. But each permission is a blast radius waiting to happen.

posts.title: AI SDRs expose the real problem
posts.hook: AI SDRs didn't replace reps at the companies I work with. They replaced the busywork that was hiding bad strategy.
posts.body:
AI SDRs didn't replace reps at the companies I work with. They replaced the busywork that was hiding bad strategy.

When you automate the send, you realize most outbound was just volume theater. 500 emails a week that all say the same thing to loosely targeted lists. The activity metrics looked great. Pipeline didn't.

The teams I've seen actually win with AI outbound did something counterintuitive. They sent fewer emails. But each one was built on real signals.

Job postings that indicate tech stack changes. Funding rounds that unlock budget. LinkedIn activity that shows a person is thinking about the problem you solve. Enrichment data layered three deep before a single email gets drafted.

One campaign I helped build: 3,200 emails sent over 60 days. 4.7% reply rate. Not because the AI wrote better copy. Because the targeting was surgical and the timing was based on actual buying signals, not "they're in our TAM spreadsheet."

The AI didn't replace the SDR. It replaced the excuse to not think about who you're emailing and why.

Signal-based outbound is just... outbound done properly. The AI makes it possible to actually do the research at scale.

A team I work with automated their outbound with an AI SDR tool. Same templates, same lists, same cadence. Just faster. They expected more pipeline from more volume.

Instead they got the same conversion rate at higher speed. Which meant they could see, clearly and quickly, that the conversion rate was terrible.

When a human SDR sends 50 emails a day and books one meeting a week, you can blame effort. Maybe they're not personalizing enough. Maybe they need more coaching. The activity metrics create enough noise to hide the real problem.

When an AI sends 500 emails and books the same one meeting, the hiding is over. The volume is there. The effort excuse is gone. You're staring at the strategy.

This team did something smart. They stopped adding volume and started adding signals. Job postings that indicated a relevant pain point. Funding announcements within 30 days. Tech stack changes visible in public data. They cut their list by 80% and only reached out when a trigger fired.

Conversion rate went from 0.4% to 3.1%. Not because the AI got better at sending. Because humans got better at choosing who to send to.

AI outbound amplifies your strategy. If the strategy is bad, it amplifies that too.

The obvious move with AI SDRs: automate the send, scale the volume, hit more inboxes. The teams that did this mostly got more unsubscribes and lower reply rates at higher speed.

posts.title: The one thing high-reply campaigns share
posts.hook: I've reviewed outbound campaigns for 20+ companies this year. The highest-reply ones all share one trait that has nothing to do with copy.
posts.body:
I've reviewed outbound campaigns for 20+ companies this year. The highest-reply ones all share one trait that has nothing to do with copy.

They all had a first-party data source feeding the targeting.

Not a bought list. Not a ZoomInfo export. A signal they collected themselves.

One company scraped job boards for roles that indicated their buyer was hiring for the problem they solve. Another tracked GitHub stars on competitor repos. Another monitored Reddit threads in their niche and enriched the posters.

The copy was fine. Not magic. Clear value prop, short, personalized with one real detail. But the targeting was the multiplier.

I build these pipelines with coding agents now. A Python script pulls signals from 3-4 sources, enriches contacts, scores them against an ICP, and stages them in a queue. The agent handles the enrichment orchestration. I review the output and approve sends.

Total cost: API fees plus my time reviewing. No $30k/year intent data platform. No 5-seat sales engagement tool.

The infrastructure to do signal-based outbound used to require a RevOps team. Now it requires a SQLite database and an afternoon.

remixes.label: signal-hierarchy
remixes.hook: There are three tiers of outbound targeting. Most teams are stuck on tier one and wondering why reply rates are dying.
remixes.body:
There are three tiers of outbound targeting. Most teams are stuck on tier one and wondering why reply rates are dying.

Tier 1: Bought lists. Firmographic filters. "Companies with 50-200 employees in SaaS." Everyone has this. Everyone is emailing the same people.

Tier 2: Intent data. Bombora scores, G2 visits, website traffic deanonymization. Better, but you're still reading someone else's signals through their lens.

Tier 3: First-party signals you collect yourself. Job postings that reveal a specific pain. Product usage patterns from a freemium tier. Community engagement that shows someone is actively solving the problem you address.

The gap between tier 2 and tier 3 is enormous. Tier 2 says "this company might be interested." Tier 3 says "this person is actively dealing with this problem right now, and here's the evidence."

I've watched teams with worse copy and worse sequences outperform polished operations purely because their targeting was built on signals they owned. The signal source matters more than the subject line. More than the personalization. More than the send time.

The question isn't whether your copy converts. It's whether you're even reaching the right person at the right moment.
remixes.cta: What signal are you collecting that nobody else in your space has access to?

remixes.label: bought-list-autopsy
remixes.hook: I ran a post-mortem on a campaign that got a 0.4% reply rate. The copy was actually good. The targeting killed it.
remixes.body:
I ran a post-mortem on a campaign that got a 0.4% reply rate. The copy was actually good. The targeting killed it.

The team had bought a list of 12,000 "VP of Marketing" contacts from a major data provider. Filters looked right. Industry, headcount, geography, title. Standard stuff.

But when we dug into who actually replied across their previous campaigns, a pattern showed up. The replies didn't correlate with firmographic fit. They correlated with timing.

The people who replied were going through a transition. New in role. Just raised funding. Posted a job that signaled they were building the function the product supported.

So we rebuilt the targeting. Instead of a static list, we built a scraper that watched for these transition signals daily. New leadership hires from LinkedIn. Job postings with specific keywords. Funding announcements.

Same copy. Same sequences. Same SDR. Reply rate went from 0.4% to 3.8%.

The list wasn't wrong. It was just stale. A bought list is a snapshot of who fit the profile at some point. A first-party signal feed tells you who fits the profile right now.

posts.title: Your CRM stages are fiction
posts.hook: Pipeline stages are the biggest shared hallucination in B2B sales.
posts.body:
Pipeline stages are the biggest shared hallucination in B2B sales.

"Discovery complete" means someone had a call. It doesn't mean the buyer is actually evaluating. "Proposal sent" means a PDF exists in someone's inbox. It doesn't mean budget is real.

I see this constantly when I build CRM automations. The data in the CRM tells a clean story. Discovery, demo, proposal, negotiation, closed. The actual buyer journey looks nothing like that.

A real deal might go: saw a LinkedIn post, lurked for two months, asked a colleague, replied to a cold email six weeks later, had a 12-minute call, went dark for three weeks, came back and bought.

Your pipeline stages can't capture that. So you end up forecasting off fiction.

What I've started doing instead: tracking engagement signals across channels and letting the data tell me where a deal actually is. Did they open the last three emails? Are they engaging with content? Did they forward the proposal internally (you can see this with link tracking)?

Behavioral signals over self-reported stages. It's more work to set up. It's also actually accurate.

The CRM isn't lying on purpose. It's just measuring the wrong things.

Not because someone entered bad data — because your pipeline stages don't reflect buyer behavior, they reflect what your sales team is comfortable admitting. Stage 3 doesn't mean 'Champion identified.' It means 'rep doesn't want to move it back to Stage 1.' Fix your stage definitions before you fix your data.

remixes.label: behavioral-signals-blueprint
remixes.hook: I stopped trusting pipeline stages two years ago. Now I score deals on five behavioral signals instead. The forecast accuracy doubled.
remixes.body:
I stopped trusting pipeline stages two years ago. Now I score deals on five behavioral signals instead. The forecast accuracy doubled.

The signals that actually predict a deal will close have almost nothing to do with what stage it's in.

Here's what I look for now:

1. Multi-threading velocity. How many people at the account are engaging, and how fast is that number growing? A deal with one champion in "negotiation" is weaker than a deal with four stakeholders in "discovery."

2. Response latency. How quickly do they reply to emails and schedule next steps? A 2-hour response time tells you more than any stage label.

3. Internal document requests. When the buyer asks for a security questionnaire, an ROI calculator, or a technical spec to share internally, they're selling for you.

4. Meeting attendance patterns. Are new people showing up to calls? Are senior people joining? Or is it the same lone champion every time?

5. Timeline specificity. "We want to implement in Q2" vs. "sometime this year" vs. radio silence on timing.

None of these live in a standard CRM dropdown. They require tracking actual buyer behavior, not rep self-reporting. But once you start scoring on behavior instead of stages, you stop being surprised by deals that "suddenly" go dark.

remixes.hook: Your CRM is a performance review tool disguised as a sales tool. And it's making your forecast worse, not better.
remixes.body:
Your CRM is a performance review tool disguised as a sales tool. And it's making your forecast worse, not better.

Reps don't update pipeline stages based on buyer behavior. They update them based on what makes their pipeline look healthy for the Monday forecast call.

Had a meeting? Move it to "discovery complete." Sent a proposal? That's the "proposal" stage. Never mind that the buyer ghosted after receiving it. The stage says proposal, so it stays in the pipeline at full value.

I built CRM automations for a company last quarter. They had $4.2M in "proposal" stage. I asked a simple question: how many of these proposals got a response within 7 days? The answer was 11%. Eighty-nine percent of their "proposal stage" pipeline was unresponsive.

The pipeline wasn't $4.2M. It was maybe $600K of real deals plus $3.6M of theater.

This isn't a CRM problem. It's an incentive problem. When you measure pipeline coverage ratios, reps keep dead deals alive. When you measure stage progression, reps advance deals that haven't actually progressed.

The fix isn't better stage definitions. It's building a parallel signal layer that tracks what buyers actually do, independent of what reps report.

posts.title: Build boring tools that solve your own problem
posts.hook: My best-performing tool started as a script I wrote to stop doing the same task manually every morning.
posts.body:
My best-performing tool started as a script I wrote to stop doing the same task manually every morning.

Every day I was opening four tabs, pulling data from three sources, cross-referencing it in a spreadsheet, and deciding which prospects to prioritize. Took 45 minutes.

So I wrote a Python script. Then the script got a database. Then the database got a scoring model. Then the scoring model got an agent wrapper. Then it became a product.

None of it was planned. I was just solving my own problem one layer at a time.

The founders I see building sustainably right now all have this pattern. They didn't start with a market opportunity. They started with a personal pain point, built the minimum thing that fixed it, and discovered other people had the same pain.

The advantage of building for yourself: you're the most demanding user. You know exactly when it breaks. You feel the friction instantly. You don't need user interviews to find the next feature.

You also don't need a co-founder, a team, or funding to start. A coding agent, a weekend, and a real problem you actually have.

The $12k MRR tools aren't coming from hackathon ideas. They're coming from people who got tired of doing something manually.

remixes.body:
The best internal tools don't start as projects. They start as one frustrated morning where you finally snap and write a script.

There's a pattern I've seen in every solo operator and small team that builds effective automation:

Stage 1: You do the task manually for weeks. You hate it but it's not bad enough to fix.

Stage 2: One morning it takes twice as long as usual. You write a script out of spite. It's ugly. It works.

Stage 3: The script breaks because the data changed shape. You add error handling and a config file. Now it's a tool.

Stage 4: You realize other decisions depend on the output. You add a database and a scoring layer. Now it's a system.

Stage 5: Someone asks how you do the thing. You realize you've built something others would pay for.

The critical insight: you can't skip stages. If you try to build stage 4 from scratch, you'll over-engineer it because you don't yet know which edge cases actually matter. The manual pain teaches you what the tool needs to handle.

Every useful tool I've built followed this ladder. The manual frustration is the requirements document. The ugly first script is the prototype. The real product emerges from running it daily and discovering what breaks.

Stop planning tools. Start scripting the task that annoys you most.

remixes.label: 45-minutes-test
remixes.hook: If any task in your daily workflow takes more than 30 minutes and involves copying data between tabs, that's not a workflow. That's a job opening for a Python script.
remixes.body:
If any task in your daily workflow takes more than 30 minutes and involves copying data between tabs, that's not a workflow. That's a job opening for a Python script.

I call it the 45-minute test. If you spend 45 minutes on the same task three days in a row, you have enough pattern recognition to automate it. You know the inputs, the transformations, and the output. You just haven't written it down in a language a computer can execute.

Here's the thing that stops people: they think automation means building a polished app. It doesn't. It means a 40-line Python script that runs in your terminal. No UI. No deployment. No architecture. Just a script that does the boring part so you can focus on the decision that requires your brain.

My first automation was embarrassing. Hardcoded file paths. No error handling. Print statements instead of logging. It saved me 40 minutes a day. That's 200 minutes a week. That's over 170 hours a year from a script I wrote in one sitting.

The compounding part is what gets interesting. Once you have one script, you start seeing automation opportunities everywhere. The second script feeds the first. The third script monitors both. Within a few months, you've built an operating system for your daily workflow without ever writing a product spec.

The barrier is never technical complexity. It's the belief that it needs to be complex.

posts.title: Week 1 vs week 16 of building with agents
posts.hook:
Week 1 of building with coding agents: spent 4 hours getting it to write a working API call.
Week 16: it runs my entire GTM pipeline overnight while I sleep.
posts.body:
Week 1 of building with coding agents: spent 4 hours getting it to write a working API call.
Week 16: it runs my entire GTM pipeline overnight while I sleep.

The learning curve isn't the model. It's learning how to write instructions that hold up without you watching.

Week 1 I was prompting like I was having a conversation. "Hey, can you pull some data from this API and clean it up?" Vague inputs, vague outputs, constant babysitting.

Week 16 my CLAUDE.md files read like SOPs. Schema definitions. Error handling protocols. Identity routing tables. Verification steps before any write. Explicit rules about what NOT to do.

The compound effect is real. Every session, the instructions get tighter. Every edge case that breaks something gets a new rule. The agent doesn't learn across sessions, but the instruction set does.

After four months my agent context is basically a junior employee's onboarding manual. And it works about as reliably as a good junior employee following clear instructions.

The people who try coding agents for a week and quit are stopping right before the compounding kicks in. The first month is painful. Month four is a different universe.

Consistency in building the context is the whole game.

The difference between a coding agent that wastes your time and one that saves 4 hours a day is entirely in how you write instructions. Not which model you use.

I've been building with coding agents for four months now. The model hasn't changed much in that time. What changed is how I talk to it.

Month 1: "Pull data from this API and clean it up." Result: something that technically runs but makes wrong assumptions about every edge case.

Month 2: "Pull data from this API. Here are the fields I need. Here's how nulls should be handled. Here's the output format." Result: works 70% of the time.

Month 3: "Here's a working example of the input and output. Here's a test that should pass. Here are three edge cases to handle." Result: works 95% of the time.

Month 4: I write constraint documents. Not prompts. Documents that describe the system's behavior, the invariants that must hold, and the failure modes to watch for. The agent runs overnight and I review the output in the morning.

The inflection point wasn't when the model got smarter. It was when I got better at specifying what "done" looks like. The skill isn't AI. The skill is writing clear specifications. Which, it turns out, is the same skill that makes you effective at delegating to humans.

remixes.label: compound-trust-loop
remixes.hook: Week 1 I wouldn't let the coding agent touch a production file. Week 16 it deploys to production while I sleep. The shift wasn't sudden. It was earned through a trust loop.
remixes.body:
Week 1 I wouldn't let the coding agent touch a production file. Week 16 it deploys to production while I sleep. The shift wasn't sudden. It was earned through a trust loop.

Here's how trust compounds with coding agents:

Phase 1: Supervised execution. You watch every line it writes. You don't trust the output. You rewrite half of it. This feels slow and pointless. It's not. You're learning the model's failure modes.

Phase 2: Verified autonomy. You let it run, then review the diff before committing. You start noticing it handles the common cases well. You only intervene on edge cases. Your review time drops from 30 minutes to 5.

Phase 3: Constrained delegation. You write rules and constraints, set it loose on defined tasks, and check the output. If the tests pass and the constraints hold, you ship it. Most of your time is writing better constraints, not reviewing code.

Phase 4: Overnight operations. The agent runs scheduled tasks. You wake up to completed work. Review is a morning ritual, not a bottleneck. You've essentially built a junior developer that works 24/7 and never forgets the rules.

Each phase requires the previous one. You can't skip to phase 4 without understanding the failure modes from phase 1. The people who say agents "don't work" stopped at phase 1. The people running overnight pipelines spent months earning each phase transition.

The compound effect is real. Every session, the instructions get tighter. Every edge case that breaks something gets a new rule. The agent doesn't learn across sessions, but the instruction set does.

After four months my agent context is basically a junior employee's onboarding manual. And it works about as reliably as a good junior employee following clear instructions.

The people who try coding agents for a week and quit are stopping right before the compounding kicks in. The first month is painful. Month four is a different universe.

Consistency in building the context is the whole game.
